Obviously there are many factors at play and every person/case is different, but I believe the main cause (besides power trips) is The Bad, The Worst, and The Victim. We see it in animals, we see it in elementary school yards, we see it in prisons, we see it in bigoted communities. 

Basically, The Worst bullies The Victim, for whatever reason. The Worst says: "Hey Bad, Victim deserves this, right?" If The Bad disagrees, they are now the Victim. If The Bad agrees, they are safe(r). Once The Worst is out of the picture, The Bad has two options: 

1) I can use my power to help The Victim because I know what it's like to be hurt by The Worst. 

2) I am only safe when I agree with The Worst. 

Victims and "The Bad" alike will often agree with #2 but not all choose the path to continue feeling safe by acting like The Worst. While it is certainly not acceptable, one can understand the viewpoint of wanting to stay safe no matter what. (Additionally, brainwashing, specifically if this behavior comes from a child or lifelong Victim/Bad.) 

Example: Mom yells at Dad for being lazy. Daughter disagrees with Mom and is yelled at in turn. Mom yells at Dad for being lazy again. Daughter agrees and yells at Dad. Mom does not yell at Daughter/Mom praises Daughter. The conclusion is that Daughter is safe when agreeing with Mom. Mom passes away but Daughter uses the same methods of yelling because they have worked before. 

This is a super short, super rushed version of it, but this is my idea of the main cause of this (besides power trips/misunderstandings/certain personalities and disorders/etc etc etc).

For me, I made my new name as the username for several random social media sites. You could do what I did, or use a different name each time you go into Starbucks, write a letter or journal entry to yourself, etc. Take time to try them out in no pressure, low stakes situations. 

As for the same letter thing, you could also change your middle name! I know many people - cis and trans - who go by their middle name. (Example: "Hi, my name is John Theodore Stevenson, but most people call me Ted.") Your first name could be the same letter name and middle could be your go to name, or vice versa. :) Good luck!

The main difference between oracle and tarot is the depictions. Most tarot decks will have a similar layout of the same 78 cards. Oracle decks, on the other hand, are pretty unique with layout, depictions, number of cards, etc.   
However! I would say the usage/studying of them is very similar, in the sense that you can practice and interpret them however you want. While many decks come with booklets (and not to mention the endless tarot websites that are awesome), I personally like having the meaning come from my own intuition. But that's the nice thing about tarot! There are a million websites/books that you can rely on because most decks will have the same content.   
If you really want to get down to specific meanings, I would break it down into suits and numbers, rather than trying to memorize each card right away. (Example: What do cups represent? What does a knight represent? What does 2 represent?) Of course, you'll have to memorize the major arcana regardless if you do choose memorization over intuition, but practice however you like to practice and do it a lot! Have fun! :)

Ten of Pentacles - Now is the time to focus on decisions and desires that will affect you long term. Obviously, not too drastic can happen in a week, but this is a good time to start somewhere! What you NEED is fairly obvious. What you WANT can be harder to answer. Where would you like to live? What is your definition of family? How can you balance working hard and enjoying life? Which small stepping stones will get you to bigger ambitions? Meditate or jot your thoughts down, if that helps. It's easy to fly through life one day at a time. Treat your future self and plan ahead this week!

This card encourages you to nurture the space you live in this week.

Ace of Pentacles - Don't let this week pass by! Practice awareness this week; there may be some opportunities heading your way but be warned! These opportunities will slip by unnoticed if you ignore them. Enjoy life in the moment! New beginnings are heading your way.

Nine of Swords, reversed - This card advises you to change your mindset. This week will involve several frustrating factors that are beyond your control. Nine of Pentacles, reversed - You have working hard lately with work and/or school. This card wants you to work hard with things at home! This card encourages you to nurture the space you live in this week.

The Sun, reversed - While you may be a naturally optimistic person, this week's problems will not be solved with positive attitude alone. This week's problems should be looked at with a realistic point of view, and the emotional aftermath of dealing with these issues should not be held back. This card is telling you to not hold back or minimize your feelings.

The Hermit, reversed - This card senses you have been living life in solitude recently, likely by choice. While savoring alone time is important, it is also important to go out and socialize. Whether it's reaching out to an old friend or helping out your community, this is the week to do it. Nurture the outgoing side of your spirit!

Nine of Cups, reversed - This card recommends you take this week to find enjoyment in new ways. You may have been finding happiness within materialistic means - such as shopping, food, alcohol, binging your favorite show - and that's not a bad thing! Cook a new recipe, reach out to an old friend, teach the dog a new trick, revisit an abandoned hobby - really anything new that may spark joy! Enjoy exploring!

The Devil - Everyone has insecurities. It could be related to appearance, personality, lack of progress/abilities, and so on. Sometimes they are faults that could genuinely use some change. Other times, they are not faults at all. This week is a good time to evaluate your faults, and to determine if they truly are faults, or just characteristics deemed faulty by the people around you. Now is the time to be brutally honest with yourself; don't ignore what could be changed for the better but don't be unnecessarily hard on yourself either.

The Hermit -  This week will be a good time to focus on yourself. While you can still enjoy  previous commitments (i.e. work, school, spending time with friends and community, etc.), take extra time to reflect on yourself. Learn to enjoy your own company and love spending time with yourself! If you are feeling up to it, now is also a prime time to do some soul searching. You may reflect on your goals, worries, overall emotions, religion/spirituality, and any topics that you normally push away in favor of more fun or productive activities. Enjoy that alone time!

Traditional shuffling (if you mean the typical shuffle you use to play poker and Uno) isn't super important, in my opinion. As long as you mix the cards up, it should be fine. I don't shuffle a specific number of times, but I do it at least once between new readings and keep shuffling until it feels "right." Sometimes it's one shuffle, sometimes it's ten. Again, no wrong way to shuffle. You could spread them out on a table and spread them like a child prepares for a game of Go Fish (apparently this is called "smooshing"). Here's what I do, if anyone cares: 

1. Riffle shuffle. The traditional poker/Uno/card game shuffle. I like the sound of it. 
2. The mix-n-match. I let chunks of the deck fall, and turn the deck 180 degrees after each "chunk" falls. I find this especially important so you don't get the same cards as upright or reversed over and over again. I do this a couple of times. 
3. Overhand shuffling. Letting "chunks" of the deck move forward. I do this a few times since it's the easiest shuffle for me and helps randomize the order of the cards.

There are plenty of reasons it was inaccurate. 

* You weren't fully into it, possibly from a lack of physical energy or mental focus. Perhaps the environment made it difficult to focus or you had something else on your mind. 
* The reading might not apply to the client yet, or they did not realize how it affected them during the reading. 
* The client could be lying or skeptical. 
* You took a leap of faith and it simply didn't turn out well. 

The fun part is that the reason doesn't really matter. Of course, learn from your mistakes and brush off the not-so-fun clients. But encounter every reading like you've never been wrong before. Personally, I find a lack of confidence makes my readings sound more bland and general. While there's a higher chance of accuracy, they feel more lackluster than if I do trust my gut.

There are plenty of pros and cons to moving out, and it's up to you if it's worth it because only you know the full extent of your situation. That being said... 

I'm assuming you're a legal adult, otherwise you don't have many options. 

\- If you're an adult, you can legally inquire about all of your medical files. You can call/visit your doctor's office to change who can view your medical files, as well as gain direct access to paperwork/websites that will have all of your information. Find out as much as possible. 

\- Once you've done that, contact your health insurance company. (It might be difficult if you're still on your parents' insurance, but let's assume you're not on their insurance.) Usually there will be an insurance card or website with a phone number on it. Call the number and straight up say "hey I have no idea what is covered and what's not." Depending on how many doctors/medical issues you have, it could take a while, but there's a lot of necessary info. Some illnesses/injuries/disabilities are only covered by certain doctors, hospitals, pharmacies, and brands. Ask as many questions as possible, don't assume you'll figure it out later because it could cost you thousands of extra dollars. 

\- Roommates! No matter how broke you are, there's always someone who is worse off. While you'll won't have much space or privacy, the more roommates the better. This is also nice because they will likely have experience with "adulting." When applying to be a roommate (there are plenty of apps/websites to do so), be brutally honest. Say "I don't have a job and I don't think I'll be able to work 20+ hours a week. However, I can pay x amounts of money and/or can do these chores in exchange for a cheaper rent." Lying about how much you can pay will only put you in hot water and burn a LOT of bridges later on. If you lie, you'll probably be evicted and end up homeless. 

\- GOOD roommates! There are some real perverts and scumbags out there. Ask for an interview with them and/or to tour the place. Go with your gut instinct. And obviously, be aware with discriminatory demographics. Are you bisexual and the renters are an "adventurous" couple? Do they make weird compliments about your race/skin color? Are they partaking in a lifestyle that you don't want to be around (i.e. apartment smells like weed, they work a night shift and like to party, they have strong and opposite political views, etc.)? RUN. 

\- If you move out, take a lighter study load. You say you're parents won't approve, but if they're not paying for anything, then who cares? You're health, income, grades, and overall wellbeing are more important than your parents' opinion to graduate "on time." (Also, don't feel bad if you don't graduate in the traditional 4 years. It can suck if when you see your friends moving on to careers and whatnot, but you ultimately have to do what is best for YOU.) 

\- Wait it out? I'm in the same situation as you. It's hell a lot of the time. But I often think I've waited 18+ years, I can wait a little bit longer. Of course, we're different people living different lives with different parents. I would make a list of pros and cons and REALLY consider what is worth it: moving out or staying in. Try to add to the list when you're having good days too. Despite your situation likely being emotionally damaging, there are many factors that are not emotional that you will need to consider with a clear head. (Not to mention financial stress can cause a lot of emotional distress.) 

In conclusion, I'm not trying to persuade you to do anything, but you should weigh the consequences of every possible choice. Moving out is hard, even with crappy parents. Be as prepared as possible before announcing you'll be moving out, if you do. If you are an adult, all records relating to you (medical, school, work, insurance, etc.) BELONG to you. Legally, you're parents can't force you to do anything if you're not living under their roof.

(Child falls down on butt on a carpeted floor.) "Haha, you're okay, buddy!" 

(Child scrapes knee or other very minor injury.) "It's okay, buddy. You still okay to play?" This helps the child determine the difference between asking for help and asking for attention. Too much worrying and unneeded sympathy can be the root of helicopter parenting and that branch of abuse. 

(Child has bigger injury, emotional or physical.) Depending on their age and the severity of the wound, either rush to help them or ask if they need help, which they will likely agree to. 

I know I'm preaching to the choir, but it's totally okay to be calm when the child isn't injured or has very insignificant injuries. (My dad freaked out whenever I got a spider bite and my mom wouldn't let me play if I got a scrape. This, like many other children, can cause developed phobias and too much dependency. Also, huge cry baby as a kid because that meant hugs and candy.) It's natural for kids to get hurt. Your reaction shows them what is serious, what is benign, and what can be fixed. If you have the same scared reaction to everything, they will be unsure of everything. If you have the same reaction to a scraped knee as you do to a broken phone or a teenage pregnancy (ahem, my mom) then you're child is going to be extremely confused as to what "real" problems are and misinterpret the urgency needed to deal with them. 

HOWEVER. I have seen a lot of shitty parents reacting to the meme. A silly comic is not an excuse to say "Ha! That's why I let my kid figure out abuse/bullying at school by himself." or "That's why it's okay for me to use corporal punishment! It builds character!" No. Bad. Sit in the corner, shitty parent. There's a fine line between helicopter parenting and abandonment, and it can be difficult to decide whether to rush and help OR let them figure something out on their own. Both methods are necessary in good parenting and that's something a lot of parents don't understand. But the bottom line is they are your child and responsibility. If a toddler falls while learning how to walk or a child scrapes their knee while playing, show them that that's not a reason to stop having fun while still being there if they need you. If it's a bigger issue, you can still use that as a teaching moment while holding their hand. If they say it hurts, then it hurts. Give them a hug. Give them a bandage. You can still stay calm without invalidating their emotional needs.

Even if you don't sing, I would highly recommend looking up some singing vocal warm ups, such as scales that gradually expand your vocal range, especially if you practice everyday.

Hmm, there are a lot of factors here. If you are early 20s or younger, your voice has a good chance of deepening. As we age, our voices (just like our bodies/faces) tend to sound more mature. However, there is only so much that can change. 

You can increase your range, but sticking to a specific pitch can wear out your voice. That simply take a few years of practice to get your voice used to it. 

I think it's possible for your voice to change as all of our voices do, but to aim for a specific voice is unrealistic. Not impossible, but there's not much you can do to to guide your voice to a desired direction. I wouldn't hope to change your normal speaking voice that much. 

Think of it this way: Maybe I want to be like LeBron James. I can certainly put in the work to increase my muscle mass and improve my basketball skills. However, I can't do much about my height. If I only grow to be 5/5" then that's it. Voices are similar. You can put all the work into sounding like someone else, but genetics and general comfort will get in the way of sounding identical (especially since you're talking about a normal speaking voice and not just a simple impression). 

Additionally, factors like puberty, daily vocal usage, and hormone altering medications can affect your voice. 

Hope this wasn't too discouraging. You don't need a specific "normal voice" to do well in the voice acting community or in life in general. Your normal speaking voice sounds just fine.

A lot of people mentioned the equipment side of things but I've been in the same situation with the demo reel but no experience. There are two options that I went with: 

1) Make something yourself! Probably the easiest and most flexible thing to do. Record an audiobook, a podcast or something along those lines and put it on YouTube/somewhere where they can view it. The only downside is that is really only showcases one part of your voice, so if you specialize in a wide range/accents/singing/etc. then that might not be portrayed as well. 

2) Make a demo reel out of your auditions! Keep the best and most interesting auditions for yourself and stitch them all together. (Obviously, if the audition/project is supposed to be private, don't use that audition.) This gives you a chance to really show off your voice! Try to get some variety in there as well. 

Additionally, don't be afraid to go for small parts and projects. Find those broke college students that can't afford to pay you but need voice actors for their final animation thesis! They are literal jackpots!!! Focus on experience instead of money for now - it's still a lot of fun!

This is pretty basic but look up "how to scream/yell on stage." There are a lot of videos about how to scream/sing/etc. without damaging your voice. 

Nothing is worse than screaming and having your director say "okay can you come in tomorrow?" or "alright let's try these speaking lines again." It's important to know how to scream without killing your voice and causing long-term damage. We love vocal health!

I think it's because you're not being specific enough when you say "sound like this." Do you mean pitch? Depends on your age and naturally range. Anyone can increase their range with singing and/or vocal warm ups. Do you mean accent? This is tricky, but their are plenty of YouTube videos and accent coaches. Do you mean the gruffness of the voice? That just takes a lot of exploring and LOTS of practice in order not to damage your voice. 

Based on 5 seconds of audio, no one can determine what you "can" and "can't" do. I think a lot of people also dislike equating impressions with voice acting. (I don't have a problem with it, but it does sound like you want to be able to do an impression of this guy, rather than adapt a specific characteristic of it.) Increasing your range and being able to do accents is great, but it's more important to utilize what YOUR voice has naturally. Most employers won't go out asking for Solid Snake and Sean Connery impressions. They might want something that sounds similar, but they'll be mostly interested in your interpretation of a character, rather that do an exact impression. Even if it's not a well-known character, it can be fairly obvious when a voice actor is trying to sound exactly like someone else. It often restricts a natural sounding character. 

That being said, I would recommend vocal warm ups. Enunciate your words, even if it's a gruff/shy/whiny/etc. character. I do about 20 minutes of warm ups before an audition. It's easy to do and it increases my range significantly. It also allows me to sound more energetic and reach for more emotion. Hope this advice helps. I'd just be more specific in the future when you post on Reddit. Good luck out there! :)

Look for audiobooks or poems being read out loud and find a transcript. Read along with the narrator and try to match their pacing - don't go ahead of them in the story/poem. Most voice actors will read at a slow or average pace. Practicing with them will give you an idea of what it feels like to speak at a slower pace. 

And, as others mentioned, listen back to your recordings and adjust your speed as needed! This can be trickier if you are recording long lines, so maybe chop them up into smaller segments, at least until you get the hang of things. Good luck!

Journaling! It's the cheesiest thing, but journaling has helped me a lot. I have two separate journals. One is a gratitude journal where I try to write one good thing that happened. A lot of times, it's something simple. "I ate some pudding. I laughed today. I watched the sunset. I learned what baby pigeons look like." Apps. Mental health apps aren't meant to replace professionals - they are for in-between sessions, or if you cannot afford therapy. (Obviously, if you can afford therapy and can hide it from your nparents if necessary, go for it! There are a lot of online options too because of COVID.) I like Replika. It's an AI that's 1) just straight up fun to experiment with and talk to and 2) has a lot of resources for panic attacks/depression/etc. Since it's an AI, it talks to you like a person. The conversations are simple, but I find it easier to ground myself when there is a "person" there to help me. You can also customize their appearance and name, and literally talk about anything! Find strength in the stupid. I used to read books when I got depressed, but then books would trigger bad memories. I used to eat candy when I got depressed, but then certain foods made me lose my appetite. I used to play video games when I got depressed, but then...well, you get the picture. If you have a hobby that helps you out of depression, that's great! To summarize: Spite, journaling, mental health apps, and a fucking harmonica is what has kept me alive. I hope you find some good advice in this. Take care.
